name: Emeka Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a field worker at Copley Growers, about four hundred hectares of broccoli, leeks and carrots, nearly all of it for two big supermarket chains. This time of year it's leeks. We're out at seven on the harvest rig, which is a long trailer you walk behind, cutting and trimming and putting them on the belt, and it goes on till three or four. My hands are cold from October to March.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran a corner shop on Station Road with my wife Grace for twenty-two years. Then a supermarket opened on the bypass, and inside three years we were selling milk and lottery tickets and not much else, so we closed. Funny thing is, now I cut leeks for the same supermarket that shut my shop. I've been at Copley four years and I'm still the slowest trimmer on the rig.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you going, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The crew, mostly. A lot of them are young seasonal workers from abroad, and they call me Uncle, which I like. What wears me down is the rejects. The supermarket wants every leek the same length, and when a load gets sent back, the foreman, Dale, is in a mood for a week. And the money, we've got about two weeks of bills in the bank, no more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good for them. I'd say it the way I say most things, there's always something new and most of it changes less than people say. I don't go online much, so it'd be at work, at the tea break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad it's not more than that. I don't use any of that stuff, I don't even bank on the phone, Grace does all of it. If it stays like a better search engine, it's nothing to do with cutting leeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. I'd keep turning up, and I'd keep hoping Dale puts me on the packhouse in January, which is indoors. Maybe I'd ask Grace to show me the online banking, but I've been saying that for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the weather forecast saying more of the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said most new things change less than people say. Has that been true for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. They said the self-service tills would close all the shops, and in the end it was the supermarket that closed mine, not the tills. Things happen, but slower and sideways, not like on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's one thing at Copley that's already changed since you started?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The carrots are all harvested by a big machine now, nobody walks behind it. When I started there were two crews on carrots. Now there's one man in a cab and Dale with a clipboard.

S0.say: I'd say fine, good for them, because most new things change less than people say. I'd mostly say it at the tea break, since I don't go online much.
S0.think: I'd be glad it's no more than that. I don't use any of it, my wife does the banking, and a better search engine has nothing to do with cutting leeks.
S0.do: Keeps turning up and hopes to be moved indoors to the packhouse in January. Thinks again about asking his wife to show him online banking, as he has for two years.
S0.feel: Calm, like a forecast saying more of the same.
S0.quote: When I started there were two crews on carrots. Now there's one man in a cab and Dale with a clipboard.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka is easy-going and sceptical of big predictions, partly from experience: change came to him slowly and sideways. He's already watched carrot harvesting go from two crews to one machine. His irony about cutting leeks for the supermarket that closed his shop came out with a laugh, not bitterness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some good, some bad, the way it always is. Companies hiring fewer beginners is a shame, but they'll do what's cheapest, and you can't stop that completely. I'd say both the bosses and the government should do a bit, not just one side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm a beginner at fifty-eight, and I got in. If they'd hired fewer beginners four years ago, I'd still be at home watching Grace do the books. So yes, it worries me for the next man like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hang on harder. I'd stop asking for the packhouse and just do the rig, so nobody thinks I'm fussy. I'd try to get faster at trimming, maybe stay an extra half hour on a Friday to practise on the rejects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Like hearing a noise in the engine that's not loud yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Practising on the rejects on a Friday. Would Dale let you do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He might laugh at me. But he's not a bad man, he'd probably say go on then, Uncle. The young ones would tease me, but I don't mind that, it's friendly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think of when you hear 'fewer beginners'?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Daniel, who's in the army. He's twenty-nine and he says when he comes out he wants a normal job. If nobody takes beginners, a soldier who's only been a soldier, where does he start?

S1.say: I'd say some good, some bad, as always. Companies will do what's cheapest, and both bosses and government should do a bit about fewer beginners.
S1.think: I'm a beginner at fifty-eight and I only got in because they took beginners. It worries me for the next man like me.
S1.do: Stops asking for the indoor packhouse so he doesn't look fussy. Stays an extra half hour on Fridays to practise trimming on rejected leeks.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, like a quiet noise in the engine.
S1.quote: If they'd hired fewer beginners four years ago, I'd still be at home watching Grace do the books.
S1.fieldNote: His centre views came through as 'both sides should do a bit'. His instinct under pressure is to keep his head down and stop asking for anything. His son leaving the army gave the beginner question a personal face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hard on the office people, and the politicians should stop shouting and sit down together. I'd say that at the rig, and Dale would agree, he says that about everything. I wouldn't post it anywhere, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think, well, now they know how it felt when the supermarket came. That's not kind, I know. But I watched office people walk past my shop to the bypass for three years, and nobody argued loudly about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much. I'd keep cutting leeks. I'd tell my daughter Esther, who's a hairdresser, that she's lucky, because nobody's cutting hair with an office assistant. And I'd keep the money tight in case the supermarkets squeeze prices again, because when people lose jobs, the supermarkets squeeze the growers, and the growers squeeze us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, plus a bit of something I'm not proud of. A little bit of told-you-so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not proud of the told-you-so. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the shop closed, a man from the council office came in on the last day and said, shame, I'll miss the place. He hadn't bought anything for two years. I'd think of him, that's all. Then I'd feel bad for thinking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the supermarkets squeeze the growers. Have you seen that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every year. Two winters ago they cut the price on broccoli and Copley cut the overtime the same week. Nobody said it was connected, but we all knew.

S2.say: I'd say it's hard on office people and the politicians should stop shouting and sit down together. I'd say it at work, not online.
S2.think: Part of me thinks now they know how it felt when the supermarket came. That's not kind, but nobody argued loudly about my shop.
S2.do: Keeps cutting leeks and keeps money tight, expecting supermarkets to squeeze growers and growers to squeeze workers. Tells his hairdresser daughter she's lucky.
S2.feel: Uneasy, with a little told-you-so he isn't proud of.
S2.quote: He hadn't bought anything for two years. I'd think of him, that's all. Then I'd feel bad for thinking it.
S2.fieldNote: A clear gap between say and think: publicly balanced, privately a small resentment from the shop closing. He was honest and a bit ashamed of it. His real worry for himself is the chain of squeezing, from supermarket to grower to worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there has to be a fair middle way, some tax on the big winners, but not so much that nobody builds anything. I'd say it the same to everyone. And I'd say thank God I'm on a farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it might be my lucky one. The job's safe, physical work's untouched. But we rent a flat above the old shop, which we sold, and if house prices boom, the landlord is the man who bought it from us. He'd put the rent up, and we'd pay him more to live above our own shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for any extra hours going, weekends, holidays, everything, to build a bit of cushion before the rent goes up. I'd ask Grace to look online for a cheaper flat, maybe out by the farm. And I'd hold off on everything else, no new coat this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mixed. Safe at work, not safe at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Paying rent to live above your own old shop. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a joke somebody else is telling. Most days I don't think about it. In your picture, with the rent going up, I'd think about it every time I climbed the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever move away from Station Road?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate to. Grace's sister is two doors down, and the barber knows me. But if it's that or not eating, we'd move, and I'd complain about it for ten years.

S3.say: I'd say there has to be a fair middle way, some tax on the big winners but not so much that nobody builds anything. And thank God I'm on a farm.
S3.think: It might be my lucky one, since my job's safe. But our landlord is the man who bought our old shop, and in a house price boom he'd put our rent up.
S3.do: Asks for every extra hour going to build a cushion before the rent rises. Gets his wife to look for a cheaper flat near the farm, and skips a new winter coat.
S3.feel: Mixed and uneasy: safe at work, not safe at home.
S3.quote: He'd put the rent up, and we'd pay him more to live above our own shop.
S3.fieldNote: Again his job felt safe and the danger came through housing. The image of paying more rent to live above his own old shop was striking and very much his. He'd move if forced but would hate leaving his street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down. Not stop, you can't stop it, but slow it down so people can find their feet. I'd say the companies and the government both owe us that, and I'd say it louder than I usually say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm finished, and quickly. There's already a broccoli robot on trial at a farm two hours away, Dale showed us a video and everyone laughed, but nobody laughed long. A robot that trims leeks the same length every time is exactly what the supermarket wants. I'm the slowest trimmer. Do the sum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know, that's the honest answer. I'd sign on, I'd ask Grace to look for anything, school caretaker, security, but your card says the hands-on jobs are going too. We'd give up the car first, it's two hundred a month all in, and I'd ask Esther if we could stay with her for a while, which would kill me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I've been closed down once. I don't think I've got another start in me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the young crew who call you Uncle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to go home, if home is better, or learn the robots if they can. They're young, they'll land somewhere. I'd say Uncle's going to sit in the park for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier things change slower and sideways. Does that still hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want it to. That's what I'd tell myself, that it'll be slower than they say, like the self-service tills. But in your picture it isn't, and I don't have the money to wait and see.

S4.say: I'd say slow it down so people can find their feet, and that companies and government both owe us that. I'd say it louder than usual.
S4.think: I'm finished, and fast. A robot that trims leeks to the same length every time is what the supermarket wants, and I'm the slowest trimmer.
S4.do: Signs on and gets his wife to search for caretaker or security work, knowing hands-on jobs are shrinking too. Gives up the car, about two hundred a month, and asks his daughter if they can stay with her.
S4.feel: Panicked. He's been closed down once and doubts he has another fresh start in him.
S4.quote: I've been closed down once. I don't think I've got another start in me.
S4.fieldNote: His usual calm 'it'll be slower than they say' gave way when the card ruled that out. Without savings, he can't wait and see, and he had no plan beyond cutting costs and leaning on his daughter. The weight of losing a second livelihood was clear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, no question. The others I can sit through. What would help is time, someone saying you've got two years, here's money while you look. And a job at the end of it that a man my age with no computer can actually do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the supermarkets. Everyone talks about AI and robots, but it's the supermarkets who decide what a leek is worth. If they get the robots, who stops them squeezing everybody?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'll probably ask Grace about the online banking this week. You've shamed me into it.

headlineQuote: Funny thing is, now I cut leeks for the same supermarket that shut my shop.
portrait: Emeka Diaz is 58 and has spent four years as the slowest trimmer on a leek harvest rig at a large vegetable grower supplying supermarkets, after the supermarket on the bypass closed the corner shop he ran with his wife Grace for 22 years. He has about two weeks of bills saved, never uses AI and leaves the online banking to Grace. Through most pictures he stays balanced and sceptical, saying change comes slower and sideways, with his real worries being rent and the chain of price squeezing from supermarket to worker. In the robot picture his calm collapses: he sees himself replaced by a leek-trimming robot and doubts he has another fresh start in him.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, which he says he couldn't sit through, because he'd lose his job fast with no money to wait.
whatWouldHelp: Time and money while he looks, such as two years' notice with support, and a job at the end that a man his age without computer skills can do.
